title: Alarka's Ring
hookLine: a mother's ring holds a message for the worst day
carry: satsang: good company is the cure for clinging
tomorrow: a book read aloud in a house where someone has died. which one?

lines: OPEN ONLY ON THE WORST DAY.
cards: Some people keep a note on their phone for bad days: a kind text, screenshotted, a list of reasons to keep going. In the Markandeya Purana, Madalasa gives her youngest son, Alarka, the old version.
A ring, with a message tucked inside, and one instruction: open this only when things are very bad. He rules, and the years go by.
Then his own brother Subahu marches on him with an allied king's army, and Alarka is losing.

teach.b: The question underneath: what do you do when you can't let go? Alarka opens the ring.
In paraphrase it says: give up attachment; if you can't, keep company with the good, because good company is the cure for it. Hindus call that satsang, the company of the good.
So he goes looking for good company and finds the sage Dattatreya, who doesn't hand him a battle plan.
He asks who, really, is suffering here, and teaches what the lullaby once taught his brothers: the self isn't the body, or the kingdom, or the losing of it. Then the twist.
Subahu, as the story tells it, never wanted the kingdom; he came only to bring Alarka to this. A neighbor tradition says something close.
In a Buddhist sutta, the Buddha's attendant Ananda suggests that good friendship must be half of the holy life. The Buddha answers: not half. The whole of it.
What the two share: good company isn't a nice extra on the way; it's the way.

teach.h: ONE FRIEND, TWO VIEWS OF SELF.
teach.b: An honest difference: Dattatreya points Alarka toward a self that was never the body or the kingdom.
The Buddha's teaching speaks of no such lasting self. They agree about the friend, and differ about what the friend helps you see.

how: Hindus speak of satsang, the company of the good, as a support on the spiritual path, often meaning gatherings to sing and hear teaching together; Buddhists speak of kalyanamitta, the admirable friend.

o: a ring-giving rite at a prince's coronation
the Purana told in the sage Markandeya's name
a manual of battle plans for losing kings

games.q: the ring, the sage and a neighbor — tap the pairs.
p: if you can't let go, keep good company
asks if friendship is half the path

s: the ring tells Alarka to fight harder
it says give up attachment, and if you can't, keep company with the good.
the Buddha calls good friendship the whole of the holy life
Ananda says half; the Buddha says not half, the whole.
Alarka's ring and the Buddha's answer teach exactly the same thing
both center good company; Dattatreya points to a lasting self, and the Buddha's teaching doesn't.

games.q: a friend reads Alarka's ring next to the Buddha's words to Ananda and asks how they fit together. what's the fairest answer?
o: same teaching; every religion says exactly this.
both put good company at the center; they differ on what it helps you see.
nothing in common; one is Hindu and one is Buddhist.
games.why: the ring calls good company the cure for clinging; the Buddha calls it the whole of the path. Dattatreya teaches a self beyond the body; the Buddha teaches no lasting self.

practice: Count, on your fingers, the people who leave you steadier after you've been with them. One finger for each person, and one slow breath for each. If you run out of fingers, keep counting on the breath.

wordCard.voice: The Markandeya. A Purana where one teaching reaches Madalasa's sons twice: in the cradle, and through a ring on a hard day.

orig.note: Sanskrit: sat-sanga, company with the good, what the ring offers when letting go is too hard.

carryVoice: Your line: satsang, good company is the cure for clinging. The ring says so. Rest well.

sources.ref: Markandeya Purana, the Madalasa and Alarka chapters (the ring's message; Subahu's attack; Dattatreya's teaching)
Samyutta Nikaya 45.2, Upaddha Sutta (Ananda: good friendship is half the holy life; the Buddha: the whole)
